sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Foundational Principle 1**: Modeled on the **Irish Home Rule League**, demanding self-government (dominion status) within the British Empire rather than immediate complete independence (Purna Swaraj).
• **Foundational Principle 2**: Spearheaded distinctively by two separate leagues to avoid friction: **Tilak's League** (started April 1916) and **Annie Besant's League** (started September 1916).
• **Foundational Principle 3**: Marked a shift from passive or petition-based politics to mass mobilization through **public meetings, pamphlets, newspapers, and educational campaigns**.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Complementary territorial jurisdiction—Tilak's league operated in Maharashtra (excluding Bombay city), Karnataka, Central Provinces, and Berar; Besant's league operated in the rest of India including Madras.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Launched in April 1916 at Belgaum; Operations restricted to Maharashtra (excl. Bombay), Karnataka, Central Provinces, and Berar.
Focused on vernacular education, linguistic states, and organizing village-level committees.
Often confused as the first all-India league; frequently tested for its exact geographical jurisdiction.
Launched in September 1916 at Madras; Operations covered the rest of India including Bombay city.
Relied heavily on her newspapers **New India** and **Commonweal**, and extensive lecture tours.
Involved prominent Moderates like S. Subramania Iyer, B.W. Wadia, and J. Arundale who joined after Congress inaction.
Faded due to the **Montagu Declaration of August 1917** promising gradual self-government, Besant's release, and absorption into the INC.
Moderate leaders accepted the reform proposals, leading to a split between Extremists/Moderates over Mont-Chelmsy reforms.
Crucial transitional phase bridging the 1907 Surat split and the subsequent Gandhian era of mass movements.

items.definition: The demand for self-government within the British Empire, granting Indians control over internal administration while retaining nominal British crown supremacy.
Powerful journals founded/edited by Annie Besant that served as principal propaganda mouthpieces for the movement.

Secretary of State Edwin Montagu announced that British policy aimed at the increasing association of Indians in every branch of administration and gradual development of self-governing institutions, which took the wind out of the movement's sails.
Lucknow Pact 1916 (Congress-League alliance) which synchronized with the peak momentum of the Home Rule agitation.

subcards.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
subcards.content:
• **Region / Zone Details**: Maharashtra, Karnataka, Central Provinces, Berar (Tilak's domain) and Madras Presidency, United Provinces, Gujarat, Bihar (Besant's domain).
• **Driving Advantages**: Leveraged urban professional networks, student bodies, and vernacular press to penetrate regions previously untouched by Congress moderate politics.

subcards.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
subcards.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Government repression (internment of Besant in 1917, ban on Tilak entering Punjab/Delhi), lack of mass peasant mobilization in certain interiors.
• **Policy Interventions**: Legal defense fund organized by leaders like Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Motilal Nehru; transition into the wider Non-Cooperation framework post-WWI.

subcards.title: Mnemonic for Classification / Sequence
subcards.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "TAM-BEL" (Tilak April Maharashtra / Besant September Madras).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Tilak started in April 1916 (HQ Belgaum); Besant started in September 1916 (HQ Madras).
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly prevents chronological mix-ups of which league started first and their respective founders.

subcards.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
subcards.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Tilak = Marathi/Vernacular roots + Village committees; Besant = Theosophical network + English/Vernacular press + All-India reach.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that Mahatma Gandhi was the president or founder of the Home Rule Leagues. Gandhi was not involved in leading either league initially; he joined the Annie Besant league later in Gujarat in 1917.

Mains Value Addition: Quote how the Home Rule movement successfully bridged the gap between the Moderates and Extremists, facilitated the historic Lucknow Pact of 1916, and trained a new cadre of leaders (like Jawaharlal Nehru) who would later lead Gandhian mass movements.

keyTakeaways: The Home Rule Movement was distinct for operating through two non-competing leagues led by Tilak and Annie Besant.
It capitalized on wartime disillusionment and successfully shifted the national struggle from petitioning to active organizational propaganda.
The movement concluded effectively following the August 1917 Montagu Declaration, which promised responsible government.
